fields.title: The Key in My Hand
fields.description: This book delves into transformative teachings on priorities, covenant relationships, and the Body of Christ. Unveil the tragic reality of strained connections, expose Satan’s devices, and explore the healing process through forgiveness and release. Encounter true stories of miraculous transformations and practical guidance for personal healing. Contents: A Covenant People—The Body of Christ—The Tragic Truth—The Devices of Satan—Unneeded Baggage—The Rock of Offense—The Wounded Soul—Our Response—The Key to Release—Heaven is Opened—Jesus – The Healer—Walking Out Your Healing.

qa.question: What is The Key in My Hand about?
qa.answer: It is a book by Gareth Evans on priorities, covenant relationships, and the body of Christ — and especially on the healing of broken relationships. It exposes the tragic reality of strained connections and the devices Satan uses to divide, and explores the healing that comes through forgiveness and release, illustrated with true stories of transformation and practical guidance for personal healing.

qa.question: Who is Gareth Evans?
qa.answer: Gareth Evans is a Bible teacher and preacher whose ministry has spanned teaching, missionary work, and conference speaking over many years. The Key in My Hand reflects his practical, Scripture-centred approach, applied here to relationships, forgiveness, and healing within the body of Christ.

qa.question: What is 'the key' the title refers to?
qa.answer: The key is forgiveness and release — the means by which broken and wounded relationships can be healed. The book's message is that the reader holds this key in their own hand: that by forgiving and releasing others, they can unlock healing for wounds and strained connections, and open the way for God's restoring work.

qa.question: What does the book teach about covenant relationships?
qa.answer: That God calls his people into covenant relationships — bonds of committed love and faithfulness — within the body of Christ, and that these are often damaged by offense and division. The book holds up the value of such relationships and grieves their breakdown, pointing the way back through forgiveness to the unity God intends for his people.

qa.question: How does the book address broken relationships and forgiveness?
qa.answer: It faces honestly the 'tragic truth' of strained and wounded connections, exposes the devices Satan uses to divide believers, and then walks through the healing process — dealing with the wounded soul, our response, and the key of release through forgiveness. It combines this with true stories of transformation and practical steps for walking out one's own healing.

qa.question: Does the book include real stories of healing?
qa.answer: Yes — it recounts true stories of miraculous transformations in relationships and lives, alongside its teaching. These accounts illustrate the book's message that forgiveness and release bring real healing, and they give the practical guidance a concrete, believable form, showing that what the book calls for actually works in people's lives.

qa.question: Who is this book for?
qa.answer: For any believer carrying the wounds of broken or strained relationships, or wanting to understand forgiveness and healing within the body of Christ. Its practical guidance and true stories make it especially useful for those seeking to be released from old hurts and to see damaged relationships restored.

qa.question: Where should a reader begin?
qa.answer: At the beginning, letting the book first set out covenant relationships and the tragic reality of division before it moves through the wounded soul to the key of release and walking out one's healing. Because it builds from diagnosis toward the healing process, it rewards being read in order and applied prayerfully.

fields.title: Personal Profile
fields.body_html:
Gareth, and his wife Anne, were both born and raised in Wales. They married in 1961 after he had received his Bachelors of Science with honors in Physics as well as a Diploma of Education from the University of Wales. In 1975 they immigrated to Canada where Gareth continued in his chosen profession as a secondary school physics teacher. In 1979 he was invited to pastor a church in Kitchener, Ontario with the Christian and Missionary Alliance.

Four years later, he received a call to Victoria, British Columbia where he pastored for the next eight years, and where they still reside. In 1990 Gareth was invited to serve as the chaplain on board the Mercy Ship, M/V Anastasis, working between Europe and West Africa. There he and Anne ministered to the crew and had many opportunities to speak at churches, pastors’ seminars, and missionary conferences.

Since leaving the ship in 1994 Gareth has traveled extensively, teaching at discipleship training schools and various conferences. Gareth and Anne have three daughters and nine grandchildren.

fields.title: Foreword by Keith Price
fields.body_html:
There can surely be no better recommendation for a book than its having stood the test of clinical trial. That such a test has been applied to the principles enunciated here is surely adequate endorsement.

As you read these pages you will sense a shepherd’s heart.

Though a man of science, this man of God has no time for ivory towers. Having gone through the fires of life’s uphill experiences himself, he understands what others feel in times of struggle.

Gareth Evans has proved these principles not only in pastoral work in Victoria, British Columbia, but also further afield in places as diverse as Mexico, Africa, Europe, and Australia where he has been invited to present the material to many different groups of churches and Christian leaders.

Because of his high view of the inspiration of the scriptures from which he draws these lessons, I am confident that they will retain their value until we, being made perfect, no longer need to take the initiative to restore broken relationships.

Keith Price Victoria, British Columbia March, 1996

fields.title: Priorities
fields.body_html:
The Covenant Feast

It was a hot, dusty day as Peter and John, disciples of Jesus, entered the city of Jerusalem. They had come to celebrate Pesach, the Feast of the Passover, and were even now following a man, carrying a pitcher of water, who would lead them to the place where the feast was to be prepared.

As the Lord had told them, it had not been difficult to find their guide, for the sight of a man carrying a pitcher of water was uncommon. That was a task usually done by the women.

He led them to a pleasant two-story house where the host greeted them warmly. When they had told him their errand, they were ushered into a large, furnished room on the upper floor.

It did not take them long to prepare the low-lying table since the requirements for the feast were well known to both. Bowls of bitter herbs were alternated with plates of apples, cinnamon, and almonds. A flask of salt water and some boiled eggs were placed beside the vessels of wine and there were several portions of the unleavened bread they called “matzah.” Soon the hour arrived and Jesus came with the rest of the disciples.

There was a buzz of excitement and animated conversation as they entered the upper room. This was to be a celebration time, the happiest time of the year for all Jews; when they were reminded again of the great faithfulness of Jehovah. Had He not delivered them from the bondage of Egypt so many years ago? Could He not still deliver them from the present oppression of the Romans?

To the disciples of Jesus this time was probably even more exciting. They were wondering if the day was near when their master would reveal Himself to the nation as the long-awaited Messiah who came to set them free as prophesied by the prophets of old. They felt they were at a strategic time in the history of their people. Indeed, this past week had been rather unusual, and things were coming to a head. It was obvious that the religious leaders were very shaken by both the teachings and popularity of Jesus.

I can imagine that the conversation of the disciples was centered entirely around the events of this past week and wondering just what significance they had. I’m sure Peter couldn’t stop talking about the triumphal entry into Jerusalem just five days earlier, when the crowds had laid their garments on the dusty road and torn branches from the palm trees to wave, as they cried out, “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord, even the king of Israel” (John 12:13).

I can imagine him, head held high, chest out, as he led the donkey’s colt, upon which the master sat. John and James, the Zealots (sons of thunder), would have been more impressed with the way their master had turned over the tables of the money changers and driven them from the temple. “Did you see the look on the High Priest’s face? Brother, was he mad!”

They all lowered themselves to a reclining position alongside the table, still happy in their celebratory mood: it was party time. Jesus looked on with pleasure as His friends celebrated, but He knew something that had eluded their understanding: tomorrow He would die.

What would you do if your doctor told you that you only had a short time to live? Of course, you’d ask for a second opinion! And if that also confirmed that you would soon leave this world, your constant companions, and friends? I know what I would do. I would quickly finish my present activities and arrange to be with those most precious to me: my wife, our daughters, and their families.

I would want to tell them how much I love them and how proud I am of them. I would encourage them to go on with Jesus, serving Him and living a life to the praise of His glory.

I would ask them if there is anything for which I need to apologize to them, any hurts, any unkind words or thoughtlessness. I would want to make very sure that there was nothing left undone that could be done in bonding our relationship one with the other.

I would find very little time to talk about trivial things such as the latest sports scores or gossip, which occupy so much of my time otherwise. Indeed, all I’d be doing would be dealing with priorities . And that night, at the paschal feast, that is just what the Lord was going to do with His disciples - deal with priorities !

His Requirements

As was customary, they had all removed their shoes as they entered this upper room. Their feet were dusty, and the sand between their toes made them feel rather uncomfortable.

Soon a murmur of discontent could be heard. The bowls of water were on a table near the door and there were towels available, but where was the servant girl whose job it was to wash their feet to refresh them? She should have been here when they arrived!

I can imagine that it must have been Peter who would be the first to speak out what they were all thinking. He is so much like me - always putting his foot in his mouth! “Where’s the girl? My feet are itching. Has someone made a mistake and forgotten to tell her? Who planned this feast? Who’s on the committee?” An embarrassed whispering would be heard as the others tried to tell him to be quiet. After all, it was the Master who had made the arrangements! And He doesn’t make mistakes; even when we cannot understand His purposes.

Jesus rose from the table and walked toward the bowls of water.

“Oh good,” thought Peter, “He’s going to call the girl.”

Jesus removed His outer garment, clothed Himself with a towel, picked up a bowl of water, and turned… towards Peter!

“Oh no,” thought Peter, “He’s going to ask me to do it!”

Instead, Jesus washes the dusty feet of Peter and then, those of all the others, including Judas Iscariot who would betray Him and bring about the suffering He was anticipating that night. Can you imagine the Lord looking up into the eyes of Judas as He washed his feet? What did He see in those eyes?

Fear? Or guilt? What did Judas see in His master’s eyes? I wonder, was he able to look? Such love!

Jesus returned the bowl and towel to their place by the door, put on His outer garment ,and turned toward the disciples.

“I give you an example,” He said, “as I have done to you, so do you to one another” (John 13:1-20).

The first priority of discipleship is servanthood . We are charged by the Lord to be servants. It is essential if we desire to be like Him, who came not to be served, but to serve (Matthew 20:28). It is the condition of greatness in the Kingdom of Heaven and an evidence of being filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18,21).

I do not think that the Lord meant for us to follow Him literally in washing one another’s feet (though that is a great blessing to experience), but rather, that we are to seek to refresh one another from the dust and dirt of walking in this world. It is impossible to live in this world without some of its dirt rubbing off on you. How seldom can one read a newspaper, watch the television, or chat with neighbors or colleagues without being infected by its poison? Gossiping and grumbling, so common even among believers, soon rob us of the joy of walking the Christian way. We need the cleansing words, the refreshment and encouragement of other believers. We need to have our feet washed! That is the purpose of Christian fellowship; however, there is often just as much ‘dirt’ thrown about among believers as among those of the world!

Not only are we called to serve one another in the Body of Christ, but we are also challenged to be servants to those who would even betray our Lord and not be one of His followers.

Jesus washed the feet of Judas knowing all that was in his heart. He saw his doubts and frustrations, knew his politicking and deceit, yet He did not hesitate to wash his feet.

When He finished this task He invited all those who would recognize Him as master, to do the same.

To have the attitude of a servant is not easy in our self-centered world. It requires humility - knowing oneself as one truly is - and acceptance of oneself. When we see ourselves ‘in Christ’ we are not threatened by what others may think of us. Who cares what others may say when we know we are pleasing to the Lord? Our confidence is in Him and in His promises.

Jesus knew what His commission was, where He had come from, and what His destiny was (John 13:3). This confidence was the foundation of His servanthood. The Father had given Him authority, had sent Him into the world, and would receive Him back again.

We have the same commission and the same destiny! The World may call us weak or spineless, trying to manipulate our servant attitude to their own ends. They will take your coat, compel you to go with them a mile, and make you their slave.

Jesus told us, if that should happen, to give them also your shirt and go the second mile! In doing so, you are removing yourself from their slavery and making yourself a voluntary servant (Matthew 5:40-41).

Shortly after Judas had left the room to do his dirty work, Jesus taught His disciples a second requirement. “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another. By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:34-35). Note that this is a commandment, not an option! Have you ever tried to measure just how much He loves you? That is the only scale by which He will measure how much you love “one another!”

It would be impossible if it were not for His grace and the indwelling Holy Spirit He gives.

“To live above with those I love, O, that will be glory! To live below with those I know - well, that’s a different story!”

(Unknown Author).

We may not like one another, but we are commanded to love one another! That means no gossiping and no backstabbing, but instead honoring, preferring one another, bearing one another’s burden, and so much more… A third requirement was placed before the disciples. “If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15). He calls us to be obedient to His word. The Old Testament prophet, Samuel, rebuked the disobedient King Saul saying, “Has the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.

For rebellion is as the sin of divination, and presumption is as iniquity and idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, he has also rejected you from being king” (1 Samuel 15:22-23).

Because Saul did not obey the word of the Lord God, he lost his kingdom and authority. When Jesus spoke to the multitudes, those who heard Him were filled with amazement for He spoke as one having great authority (Matthew 7:28-29).

We who recognize Him as Saviour must also acknowledge that He is Lord. What He says has the greatest of authority.

We need to be sensitive to hear and recognize His voice day by day. He said that we, His sheep, should recognize His voice. Above all, we should hear Him speak to us through the Scriptures and obey what He says. All believers should be students of the written Word, living in obedience to its precepts.

Jesus’ requirements for His disciples are that we serve one another, love one another, and obey His Word.

His Promises

Besides the three requirements He placed before His disciples, Jesus also promised them rich blessings. He would come again and receive them to Himself having prepared a place “in [His] Father’s house” (John 14:2) for them. They would do greater works than He did as He would send them another Helper and would answer the prayers they asked according to His will. They were to know the blessing of being in Christ , and to experience the Father’s love.

The Helper, the Holy Spirit, would come to dwell in them and would lead them to the truth and knowledge of God’s will; He would bring to their remembrance all they had been taught by Jesus.

“Let not your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me” (John 14:1).

“Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid” (John 14:27).

“These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full” (John 15:11).

He promised them - and us - a peace that the world cannot give or take away, a joy whose measure is fullness, and a presence who is none other than the Spirit Himself, never to leave us or forsake us (Deuteronomy 31:6).

Have you experienced these in your walk with the Lord? I certainly have, but I long for more!

The experience of these promises is contingent on us being servants , lovers , and obedient to His Word.

fields.title: A Covenant People
fields.body_html:
The Agape Feast

“Jesus took bread and when He had given thanks, He broke it and said, ‘This is My Body, broken for you. Take and eat!’”

(1 Corinthians 11:23-24). They all did and, in so doing, identified themselves with the Body of Christ.

“In the same way He took the cup also, after supper, saying, ‘This cup is the new covenant in My blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me’” (1 Corinthians 11:25-26). I am struck that none of those present asked Him what He meant when He said this. I can only assume that they all understood.

A covenant is an agreement between two parties. “You do this for me, and I’ll do that for you!” Today, when men make covenants it is essential that proof be available in the form of signatures attached to the written agreement. Sadly, the word of a gentleman is no longer acceptable. In the time of Jesus, covenants were sealed over a common drink. It would not have been blood, as more recently among the Native Indians of North America and the tribesmen of Africa, though all the covenants of the Old Testament days would have been signified by the shedding of blood in the slaying of a sacrificial animal. Indeed, one was said to ‘cut the covenant’ rather than make one.

I do not now believe that calling the elders has anything to do with their prayer power, but rather their authority . This verse must be linked with Paul’s warning above, as they are the only verses that give any reference to reasons why believers may be sick or weak. Of course, we also are subject to germs, diseases, and sickness just as anyone in the world, but Paul’s warning must be strongly expressed to believers.

Having taught His disciples the priorities of His heart, our Lord lifted His eyes toward Heaven and spoke to His Father.

They are not of the world, even as I am not of the world. As You have sent Me into the world, I have also sent them into the world. I have given them Your glory… that they may be one … as We are One. God’s name was revealed to Moses when they met on Mount Sinai; therefore, we can be certain that He is “ The Lord God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering and abundant in goodness and truth, keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin” (Exodus 34:6-7).

Truly, Jesus manifested these same attributes to all He met.

I cannot take even one page out of the Bible and use it as an evangelical tract to give to an unbelieving friend. I can quote from John 3 or follow “The Romans Road” which explains to them the way of salvation. I can give them the “Four Steps” or “God’s Wonderful Plan of Salvation,” but I cannot tear one page out of the Bible and give it away as a gospel tract.

However, I can take whole chapters and even books, to point out God’s priorities to the believer: His way of salvation. He has declared that when His people are walking in unity as servants , as lovers and in obedience , the world will know and believe !

We are His Gospel tract! It’s time we got our priorities right and in line with His priorities! We are quick to speak when we detect heresy of doctrine in one another - isn’t it time we were just as quick to act against heresy of practice, seeing the many divisions among believers, so evident to the world?

“For the anxious longing of all creation waits eagerly for the revealing of the Sons of God” (Romans 8:19).

fields.title: The Body of Christ
fields.body_html:
One Body

“So we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another” (Romans 12:5).

The apostle Paul takes up the theme of the Lord’s upper room prayer to teach us that the relationship called for in one-to-the-other serving and loving, is best demonstrated in the example of a living body. He sees the church as the living Body of Christ instituted by God. It is not a man-made organization, but a God-made organism - a living, vital reality. It is the training and exercise ground for serving and loving. This is why Christian fellowship is so important.

John Donne, a sixteenth century Anglican priest, wrote, “No man is an island, entire of itself; every man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main. If a clod be washed away by the sea, Europe is the less, as well as if a promontory were, as well as if a manor of thy friend’s or of thine own were: any man’s death diminishes me, because I am involved in mankind, and therefore never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee.”

His sentiments could well be those of a member of the Body of Christ, recognizing his interdependence on all other parts of that body.

Islam teaches that Mohammed was called by God to complete what Jesus failed to do! Muslims recognize Jesus as a great prophet, second only to Mohammed, but they believe He failed in that He was not able to make all people into one nation. Islam calls peoples of all nations to be one as Muslims. They have failed to understand that the unity Jesus came to bring was for those who are members of His kingdom, and not one of this world. How tragic that there is such obvious disunity in that kingdom. No wonder Islam is growing so rapidly!

At conversion, the new birth, we were, “by one Spirit all baptized into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13). This includes Baptists, Anglicans, Pentecostals, and whatever group you belong to. Not the denominations, but the individuals within all such groups who know the Lord as a personal Savior, and know their sins are forgiven through the work finished on Calvary. The baptism into the Body must not be confused with the baptism into the Spirit, experienced by the disciples on the day of Pentecost, and by many since that day. The former is “by the Spirit into the Body” whereas the latter is “by the Lord Jesus into the Spirit” (Luke 3:16). We are to be “in Christ” for justification, and Christ is to be “in us” for sanctification.

Fullness of the Spirit

One major division in the body is due to various doctrines concerning this baptism of the Spirit.

Are tongues the initial evidence of being so filled? Are they evidence at all? I am not getting into that argument except to say that, whichever view we hold, we should not make our disagreement a cause for division, that way we are certainly not exhibiting the reality of any fullness of the Holy Spirit!

He comes to make the presence of Christ, and His will, real to us. He leads us into truth. I find it rather striking that, when Paul exhorts us to be “filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18), he follows by giving us three evidences of a life so filled: 1. A worshiping attitude speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord (Ephesians 5:19).

2. A thankful attitude always giving thanks for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God, even the Father (Ephesians 5:20).

3. A servant attitude and be subject to one another in the fear of Christ (Ephesians 5:21).

Don’t tell me that you are a Spirit-filled Christian unless these three are evident in your life!

Paul then continues in his letter to the Ephesians by showing how this third evidence is worked out in our relationships as: husband and wife, children and parents, and workers and masters (Ephesians 5:22-6:9).

The Local Church

I am not among those who consider denominations as such to be evil. I believe that the Lord established most of them to enable us to mature as believers within a group of people most like us in personality and persuasion; however, when our groupings cause us to be divided from those within the Body of Christ who do not share our opinions concerning styles of worship, interpretation of Scriptures, and emphases, we are in danger of bringing condemnation upon ourselves. We may not like one another, but we are commanded to love one another!

There are three major Scripture portions where the apostle outlines his understanding of the Body of Christ.

1. Ephesians 4:1-16 → We are challenged to walk in a manner worthy of our calling showing humility, gentleness, patience, love, and being diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. For, he declares, “There is ONE BODY” (Ephesians 4:4). He continues by writing about some of the grace gifts in verse seven given to that Body. They are ministry gifts of apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers, which are given “for the equipping of the saints… unto maturity” (Ephesians 4:13).

2. Romans 12:1-8 → We are challenged again to give ourselves as living sacrifices with renewed minds. All members of the Body do not have the same function, but we are all interdependent on one another. We all have different grace gifts (Romans 12:6) with which to serve one another.

Therefore, we must, “Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good. Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor” (Romans 12:9-10).

3. 1 Corinthians 12-14 → We cannot separate chapters 12 and 14 from that great chapter on love, chapter 13! The first chapter deals with the doctrines of the Body and the charismata given to that Body. Note that these charismata are given to the individual, not for their own use, but for the benefit of the whole Body!

Then Paul expands on his teaching concerning the Body by showing just how foolish it is for one part of the Body to claim that they do not need the other parts! The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you” or again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you” (1 Corinthians 12:21). We need one another!

At the end of this chapter, he gathers together the lists of grace gifts he recorded in Ephesians and Romans showing them all to be among his long list of charismata .

Such gifts are of little value unless exercised with love (1 Corinthians 13) and properly in an orderly manner (1 Corinthians 14).

Are you fully functioning in the Body of Christ? Are you grounded in a local church, serving others, loving others, and obedient to His Word? If your ministry is wider than the local church, are you in the right relationship with God to appoint leaders, and be accountable to them as a member of the same local expression of the Body?

Some might seek to be an arm reaching out, others a voice speaking to this world, but I often see myself as nothing more glamorous than a big toe! As a former pastor, I was often working in dark and smelly places, feeling under pressure, dealing with peoples’ problems (sand between the toes).

However, I feel I am privileged when asked to minister because I get to bring balance to the Body. That surely, is the main function of the big toe!

fields.title: The Tragic Truth
fields.body_html:
God’s desire, and the priority on the heart of Jesus, is that He will have a people whose love for one another, and attitude of servanthood will be such a witness to this world that men and women will be crying out to know our Lord. They will want to know the secret of our peace, joy, and harmony. They will watch our marriages, homes, children, and workplaces, not to criticize, but to know our secrets.

Having urged his readers to be “filled with the Spirit,” and expressing one evidence of being so filled, as being “subject to one another in the fear of Christ” (Ephesians 5:21),Paul gives examples of how this should be in our relationships.

Christian Marriage → Ephesians 5:22-33

If Christian marriages were what they are supposed to be, with both parties Spirit-filled and submitted to one another, honoring, and preferring the other, they would be the mystery revealed to a watching world. Men would see the relationship that Jesus has with His bride, the church, and would be drawn to know Him as the foundation for his marriage also. There would be a steady path of seekers coming to our home or church door, rather than rushing, as they now do, to the divorce courts!

Women would want to honor their own husband above all other men, because of the love they receive, and men would want to love their wives because of the honor they receive.

Rather than a vicious circle of abuse and retaliation which is so common in the world, there would be a delicious circle of blessing one another in Christ.

It is so tragic that divorce is so common among Christian believers. What kind of witness is that?

The Christian Home → Ephesians 6:1-4

Where parents are in the right relationships with the Lord and with one another, their children mature in a secure, loving home. Most of the counseling I do as a pastor has to do with wounds received by children growing up in a rather different situation, though often “Christian” fathers fail to disciple (or discipline) their children and, instead, provoke them to anger (Colossians 3:21).

Christian counselors today speak of dysfunctional families where the child’s ‘love tank’ is not filled with the love it was created to receive, because the dysfunctional parents are incapable of providing that love. The child does not experience the love whose fruit is security, identity, self-esteem, acceptance, and encouragement. The child does not experience the love whose fruit is security, identity, self-esteem, acceptance, and encouragement.

Instead of growing up emotionally and spiritually healthy, they become just like their parents, dysfunctional. They never learn to walk tall in a world of bowed shoulders and broken hearts. The empty space in their love tank is filled with one thing: anger, which produces a life of rebellion to God’s purposes. Such children never learn to obey their parents in the Lord.

“Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger” (Colossians 3:21).

It is so tragic that so many rebellious children are the product of “Christian” homes. What kind of witness is that?

The Workplace → Ephesians 6:5-9

The Spirit-filled believer is called to be a witness in his workplace by displaying the attitude of a servant before his co-workers and employers and should be trustworthy to do his work well.

Be very sure of this! If it is the Lord’s priority to have a people in right relationships with one another in obedience to His Word, it certainly is Satan’s priority to mar such relationships! “Divide and conquer,” might as well be his motto.

fields.title: The Devices of Satan
fields.body_html:
When Jesus died on the cross and then rose again, He conquered Satan and his demonic hosts, taking away all their power, “having disarmed the powers and authorities He made a show of them openly” (Colossians 2:15). They now wage war through lies, deceit, and fear which he works into all areas of our lives: our attitudes, emotions, thoughts, and even the physical.

However, they only have power in these areas as we give it to them! The apostle Paul declared that we are not ignorant of his devices (2 Corinthians 2:11), but unfortunately that is just not true for the majority of believers today!

The Devil’s Opportunity

Have you ever been angry? Of course you have. Me too. And so was Jesus when He saw the money changers in the temple.

I’m sure He was also angry when He saw the multitudes in deep poverty and with much sickness. His heart grieved when He saw the results of the disobedience of Adam falling on all mankind. The feeling of anger is not sin. Feelings are not moral or immoral - they are amoral. What we do with our feelings, however, does matter, greatly. Paul exhorts us that when we are angry we must not sin. Then continues to add, “and do not let the sun go down on your anger” (Ephesians 4:26).

We must deal with the situation right away. If we allow the anger within to fester, it will produce a bitterness that will rob us of God’s best. As long as we are in this world, people will do us wrong, and offenses will come. Jesus warned us of that (Luke 17:1). There might be a ‘good’ cause behind our anger within us, but He has given us His Holy Spirit to enable us to know grace in those times.

“Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord. See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no ‘root of bitterness’ springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled” (Hebrews 12: 15).

If we do not deal with the anger in the appropriate way (which we will discuss later), we are playing right into the hands of the enemy! Paul continues by saying “and do not give the devil an opportunity” (Ephesians 4:27). Later, in the same portion of Scripture dealing with our conversations with one another, he warns us that we may be grieving the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 4:30).

When we bear anger (or other wrong attitudes), the enemy has access to our thoughts, spreading his lies and deceit to drive a wedge further in. Soon it appears that reconciliation is impossible, and he has won that battle.

Jesus warned us to be on our guard (Luke 17:3) and Paul charged us to be sure that no advantage be taken of us by Satan (2 Corinthians 2:11). Both are in the context of forgiveness to those whom we perceive as having wronged us. An attitude of unforgiveness (like anger) gives the enemy an advantage - an opportunity - a foothold in our life. The opposite attitudes of forgiveness and peace defeat him.

The Roaring Lion

Have you ever seen a lion stalking its prey? I haven’t, but I assume it is much like my cat stalking the birds or mice in our garden. He crouches very low and moves very slowly so as not to warn his intended prey of his intentions. He certainly doesn’t let them know he is coming by making a loud meow!

What, then, does the apostle Peter mean when he tells us to “Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8)?

In “Pilgrim’s Progress” by John Bunyan, we read that Pilgrim was approaching the Palace Beautiful which was built for the relief and security of believers. He now understood why Timorous and Mistrust, others seeking the Celestial City, had fled past him in great fear, for the entranceway was guarded by two lions.

Immediately, Pilgrim’s heart sank and he also became afraid.

If a lion came bounding into your room and roared at you, I imagine you would react like them - full of fear! I would!

Roaring lions have that effect on us - they are very frightening.

Soon, Pilgrim noticed that both lions were chained and that, so long as he walked a narrow path between them, neither could reach him to cause him harm. We need to understand that the lion, Satan, has had his teeth pulled and is chained.

He cannot harm the people of God so long as we keep to the narrow way. Even when we step off the narrow way, the Father’s love reaches out to bring us back before the enemy can destroy us. However, he will roar, and many are defeated by their emotions reacting to the roar.

His roar is often that of the accuser, bringing condemnation.

It was the first time Mary had sung the solo parts in the youth choir. It went well except for that high note in the chorus where she was a little weak and wobbly. It was only a quiet voice whispering in her ear that told her, “You made a fool of yourself,” but it was the roar of the lion. She vowed never to sing in public again.

Pastor John had such high hopes when he began ministry at St. Peter’s church. Now, just two years later he was leaving.

The youth group had not grown in numbers as the senior pastor had expected, so John was invited to leave. The lion roared, “you’ll never be successful as a pastor. You’re a failure!” A week later, he reapplied for the secular job he had left when he first believed that God had called him into the pastorate.

Alec had slipped again. He so longed to be free from this filthy habit of smoking, but it was too tempting when he’d been offered this cigarette. Now he was feeling guilty, and the lion roared, “God can’t use you. You’re always letting Him down!”

Not only does the lion roar at every slip or failure, but he knows which of our emotions are the most likely to be affected by the roar. For some it is the emotion of guilt, for others, it’s fear. Many react to his roar in the emotions of low self-esteem, lacking confidence. Where do you react?

How sad when the roar of the lion comes through the thoughtless comment of another believer! It is important in the Body of Christ to affirm one another to counteract the lies - the roar of the devil!

The Archer

When one is about to wage a battle, it is good to occupy the high ground. This enables you to see their moves so that you can take the appropriate steps to counteract them. We need to understand as believers, the tremendous privilege we have of being “in Christ.” Paul declares that God has “exalted Jesus, far above every rule and authority and power and dominion” (Ephesians 1:21).

To the Jews, these are the names of the ranks of the demonic army of Satan, but all of them are far beneath His feet. He has crushed the head of their master and has all authority over them. He wills us to exercise that authority so that we may learn to be overcomers. Those that would reign with Him must be worthy to wear a crown, and crowns are only to be given to the overcomers.

“[Christ has] raised us up with him and seated us with him in the Heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:6).

We must live on that higher ground where the only way Satan can reach us is by firing his fiery arrows. We have also been provided with a sure defense against those flaming missiles when Paul writes, “In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one” (Ephesians 6:16) As the enemy would throw his lies and accusations against us, we hold up our shield of faith, remembering that “faith comes by hearing… the Word of God” (Romans 10:17).

We need to know who we are and the privileges of being “ in Christ .”

I am… ● A child of God (John 1:12).

● A friend of Jesus (John 15:15).

● A joint-heir with Christ (Romans 8:17).

● Joined to the Lord (1 Corinthians 6:17).

● A member of His Body (Ephesians 5:30).

● Reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:18).

● God’s handiwork (Ephesians 2:10).

● A citizen of Heaven (Philippians 3:20).

● A new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17).

● Chosen by God (Colossians 3:12).

● A saint (Ephesians 1:1).

● A stranger to this world (1 Peter 2:11).

● What I am (1 Corinthians 15:10).

● Satan’s enemy (1 Peter 5:8).

● Clothed in righteousness (Ephesians 4:24).

● God’s dwelling place (1 Corinthians 3:16).

● A member of a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, and a people for God’s own possession (1 Peter 2:9-10).

In Christ I… ● Am completely forgiven (Romans 5:1).

● Am greatly blessed (Ephesians 1:3).

● Am chosen to be holy (Ephesians 1:4).

● Am sealed by His Spirit (Ephesians 1:13).

● Am predestined to be His child (Ephesians 1:5).

● Have Christ within me (Colossians 1:27).

● Am made complete (Colossians 2:10).

● Am bought back from Satan (Ephesians 1:7).

● Am seated in Heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6).

● Am free from condemnation (Romans 8:1).

● Have direct access to God (Ephesians 2:18).

● May come to God confidently (Ephesians 3:12).

For a more complete list, read your Bible!

It used to be that there was a simple remedy for most minor ailments, “Just take two aspirins and go to bed!” Today, I have a simple remedy for most of the minor attacks of the enemy to offer.

Take two of the above Scriptures each day and meditate on them. Your faith will soon grow strong, and the fiery arrows will be less effective against you.

fields.title: Unneeded Baggage
fields.body_html:
“Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us” (Hebrews 12:1).

Many are hindered in the battle, not because of the roaring lion or the arrows of lies, but because they have taken upon themselves a burden that they should not be carrying; they have been offended by someone and have taken umbrage.

I was at a viewing place, looking down on Gibraltar. There were many signs warning viewers not to feed the small monkeys that lived in the surrounding trees. Of course, some people chose to ignore the signs with the result that soon, a monkey would land on one’s shoulders. While cameras were in action, the monkey would begin to tangle its fingers in the hair so that, when it became painful, the recipient found difficulty in its removal.

Satan has an army of trained ‘monkeys’ ready to jump on one’s shoulder to tangle their fingers in their victim’s hair.

We need to recognize the monkey of offense and quickly remove it before it robs us of our peace.

Many are hindered in the battle, not because they have been ‘wounded’ by others, but because they have taken upon themselves a burden that they should not be carrying. They have been offended by someone and have ‘taken umbrage.’

We must realize that offense and sin are very different.

Though the former may be a ‘fruit’ of the sinful life, it is not a deliberate sinful act of the one who offends. Indeed, we are told that Jesus was an ‘offense’ to the religious leaders of His time, and He was without sin. It is my belief that He deliberately caused offense on more than one occasion, as I shall present to you shortly.

There may be many causes for offense, but the following are the most common: ● Personality clashes : People will often use this phrase as an ‘excuse’ for not getting along with one another!

● False expectations : Probably, the number one reason pastors and churches separate. We are not very good at making our expectations known before offense occurs.

● Misunderstandings : Poor communication.

● Gifts and talents : I often see people envy others’ prominence, instead of feeling secure in their own ministry or ‘calling.’

● Pride : An affront to one’s ‘ego.’ (for example: a father who is angered (offended) by his son’s average grades in school, believing it reflects poorly on himself).

● Rebellion : The ‘old man’ refuses to die!

A great example of these offenses at work was when a church was undergoing a renovation - they were rebuilding their sanctuary. It had been two long years of hard work for the congregation who were building this church, but God had proven Himself to be faithful.

There were many stories of ‘miracles’ of provision from Jehovah Jireh. It was now time to decide the color scheme for the interior of the sanctuary, so a small committee was formed of members of the church and John, art master at the local school, was asked to lead the group. At their first meeting, John arrived with a portfolio outlining his suggestions (some say ‘decisions’) for the color scheme. It was not long before others present expressed their disagreement with his proposals, having some opinions of their own.

Finally, a vote was taken and a consensus decision made - that did not reflect the art teacher’s views. John was offended and the reverberations of his offense were felt in that church for some time afterwards. Indeed, some even said that that was when the ‘miracles’ ceased.

John is no different than all of us! It is so easy to be offended without realizing the terrible negative impact this can have on ourselves and on the work of Christ. It is a major weapon used by Satan in defeating us in the battle. Be sure of this - offenses will come (Luke 17:1). Jesus told us of their certainty and warned us how we can be kept from stumbling at the offense: by responding to His requirements for discipleship, made in the Upper Room Let us look at some Biblical examples of people who were offended. We shall seek the cause and note the results of their offense. Hopefully, we shall also discern the Lord’s purposes in allowing the offenses to come. He has promised to deliver us from the ‘evil one,’ but has never promised to deliver us from offenses! He would, however, teach us to recognize the offense and to receive His grace in such times of testing.

The various translations of the New Testament can confuse us on this topic, so let us understand that the Greek word, “skandalon” is variously translated as “a stumbling block.” In other words, “an offense,” or “a falling away.”

The Sower and the Seed → Matthew 13:18-21

In the verses above, Jesus teaches a crowd this well known parable as well as interprets the parable for them, likening the four types of soil to four types of hearers of the God’s Word.

The ‘stony places’ describes the person who “hears the word and immediately receives it with joy, yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while, and when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately he falls away” (Matthew 13:20-21).

This is a believer who doesn’t like what the Bible teaches him. He had anticipated that being a Christian would be easy!

He wanted joy and peace, but wasn’t prepared to take up his cross (Matthew 16:24), to pay the price of servanthood. By and by, he is offended and falls away, the result being no fruit !

A Prophet Without Honour → Matthew 13:54-57

Jesus came to His own town of Nazareth where He taught in the synagogue. His neighbors were astonished at His teaching, questioning where He received such wisdom. “Isn’t this the carpenter’s son?” they said. “We’ve known him since childhood! Who does he think he is?” There is a common phrase, ‘familiarity often breeds contempt’ and as we read in verse 57, those from Jesus’ hometown “took offense at Him.”

How many young men and women, responding to God’s call on their lives, have tried to answer that call, but have been hindered by the greater ‘wisdom’ of their neighbors:family, friends, and church leaders! I am reminded of the old prophet in 1 Kings 13 who was offended because God was using another young man to proclaim His word. Because of his offense, the old prophet deceived the young man, the result being the silencing of his witness, through death!

As a result of their offense in Nazareth, “he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief” (Matthew 13:58). A sure way to stop the Lord moving in miraculous ways in your life, is to take offense. The result of their being offended was no miracles !

The Betrayer → Matthew 26:6-14

Jesus was at the home of Simon, a leper, when a woman came in with an expensive box of perfumed ointment. She broke it over the Lord’s feet and began to wipe them with her hair, so that the fragrance filled the house. Matthew tells us that the disciples were offended when they saw this ‘waste,’ declaring that the perfume could have been sold for a high price and the money given to the poor (Matthew 26:8).

Just after this, Judas Iscariot went to the chief priests in order to betray his master (Matthew 26:14-16). In John’s account of this event, we are told it was Judas himself, who made the complaint, being offended, “not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the money bag he used to help himself to what was put into it” (John 12:6).

I remember when a well-known international charity spent over one million dollars to make a documentary film about their work. Many of their supporters expressed indignation at such ‘waste’ and withheld their monthly contributions. They felt themselves to be justly indignant; however, within one year, the proceeds from the showing of that film, exceeded five times the cost of making it! I believe we should rather be on the cautious side when we come to spend the Lord’s money, but taking offense could be a greater source of embarrassment!

Judas was offended, so he went out to betray his master. The potential for betrayal was already there, but the offense stirred that potential into action. The result of his offense was that he no longer trusted the Lord to do what He said He would. Judas would goad Him into action. If He were the promised Messiah who would establish His kingdom in place of the Roman empire, now was the time to prove it! But only one thing was proved - that he, Judas, was a poor politician and an even poorer friend!

Judas had lost confidence in the Lord! Where is your confidence placed? What do you place your trust and your hope in? Christian ‘hope’ is an eager expectation that what He has promised, He will complete! The hymnist declares “My hope is built on nothing less than Jesus’ blood and righteousness!” (My Hope is Built On Nothing Less, Robert Critchley).

The writer of Hebrews encourages us to “not throw away [our] confidence, which has a great reward” (Hebrews 10:35).

When we are offended, a lack of hope will be the result, and therefore, we will have no confidence !

Peter’s Denial → Matthew 26:31-35, 69-75

Jesus had just come to the Mount of Olives, having instituted the communion covenant with His disciples. He now teaches them that He is about to be taken away from them.

Jesus tells His disciples, that “You shall all be offended because of Me tonight.” But Peter, being brave and foolish, says, “I will never be offended in You, even if everyone else is!” (Matthew 26:31-33). How he must have regretted those words just a few hours later! I feel for Peter because he is so much like me! How wonderful a Savior we have who, feeling his pain, would appear first to Peter after His resurrection, and before the others saw Him (Luke 24: 34). I can only imagine that scene as the two of them were reconciled through the Saviour’s love.

John and Peter entered the house of the High Priest where Jesus was being tried. As Peter passed through the doorway a slave girl said to him, “Aren’t you one of His disciples?” He responded, “I am not!” Then two more times he denies his Lord, adding some choice oaths before the roosters crow.

I like to imagine that young slave girl and her question. Could it have been possible that she was interested in the Lord and wanted to know more about Him? If Peter had acknowledged his discipleship, would she have asked him to tell her about his friend since she wanted to love Him also? However, Peter was offended , and the result of his offense was no testimony !

Many Turn Away → John 6:53-61

In this passage, Jesus is speaking some hard things to His followers. He is calling them to “eat of My flesh and drink of My blood” (John 6:53). Today, in retrospect, we understand this in terms of the communion cup and the new covenant He has called us into, but to them it was a hard saying which was difficult to understand.

Jesus asked them, “Are you offended?”

Are you offended by His call to the discipleship demanded in the communion covenant? The discipleship which is the core challenge of this book? The result of their offense was that many of His disciples went back and walked no more with Him (John 6:66). The result of their offense was no community.

So we have five Biblical examples of those who were offended, with the result that they lost their fruit , confidence , and testimony . Within them there was disunity, and God didn’t do any miracles among them! Therefore we can be sure Satan must have gloated.

fields.title: The Rock of Offense
fields.body_html:
Jesus was the cause of much offense! Both Peter and Paul quote the Old Testament in calling Him “a rock of offense” (Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:8).

The Pharisees were offended by Him, demons were offended by Him, and even His family was offended by Him!

But to some He deliberately avoided offending such as the despised tax gatherers. He told Peter to go to the sea where he would find the required tax in the mouth of a fish, “so that we do not give them any offense” (Matthew 17: 24) But to others He seems to deliberately offend!

John the Baptist - Jesus’ Cousin

John the Baptist was second cousin to Jesus and had been born just a few months before Him. He was full of the Holy Spirit even while in his mother’s womb and was the first to show any response to the promised Messiah. He had leapt in Elizabeth’s womb when Mary, the mother of Jesus, had first come to tell the remarkable story of her baby’s conception.

I’m sure the two boys must have spent many hours together during childhood. They had probably played and worked together, run and fought together, and talked and argued together. Perhaps they even talked together about the burden that was growing in each of their hearts.

Finally, John leaves home to answer a strange compulsion. It could have been possible that Jesus was the only one who understood when he announced that he must “prepare the way of the Lord” (Matthew 3:3), and then he left for the desert.

There, John began to preach to all who would listen to him.

“The Messiah is coming soon” he would proclaim, “and we are not ready! Repent and be baptized. Return to your God!”

(Matthew 3:2-12) The people responded, seeking to be reconciled to Jehovah and indicating their new resolve by being baptized in the local stream, the River Jordan. Theirs was a baptism of repentance and a return to orthodoxy.

One day Jesus came to the Jordan River and John cried out to the people, “Behold the lamb of God who takes away the sin of the World!” (John 1:29). John gave witness that he saw a dove descending upon Jesus and remaining upon him.

Moreover, the Holy Spirit had already told John that this would be the sign of the coming Messiah in John 1:34 where it’s written “I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God.”

John was not a popular preacher who ‘tickled men’s ears.’

Most of those who came to hear and see him were looking for a curiosity, hoping that they would be there to hear his condemnation of the self-righteous leaders of the synagogue.

He had some choice things to say to such leaders and the people loved it; however, Herod did not. He was the ruler of the Roman Empire at the time, and was a wicked man who was having an affair with his sister-in-law - an affair that John openly condemned. To silence his voice Herod had John sent to prison.

I can imagine the thoughts of John while in those dungeons.

“Herod, you old fool! You think you are in control and that putting me in prison will silence my voice. But my cousin is the Messiah and He has come to overthrow your little empire and to establish His own kingdom! He’ll get me out of this prison soon, and you will be the one locked away! He has declared that He has come to set the captive free. I can hardly wait to see your face when He does it!” And with that, John sits back in his cell and waits… and waits… and waits… Meanwhile, Jesus continues with His ministry in the nearby villages, not even finding the time to visit John in prison!

Surely, He would at least come to visit him! But because He doesn’t come, John gets offended and subsequently was beheaded! John’s disciples are sent to Jesus to ask a pointed question. “Are you truly the Messiah or should we wait for another?” (Matthew 11:3). “You do not meet our criteria since You are not doing what we expected You to do!”

Jesus replies, “And he answered them, “Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. And blessed is the one who is not offended by me” (Luke 7:22-23).

Jesus’ Dear Friend Mary

Jesus had some very special friends who lived in the small town of Bethany. He was just a few miles away when He received news that His friend Lazarus was dying and that his sisters Mary and Martha were grieving for him. “Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was” (John 11:5-6).

We do not read of any miracles, any teaching, or anything that He did during those two days! And Lazarus died! When Jesus finally came to Bethany, Lazarus had been in the tomb for four days and his sisters were in deep sorrow. It is Martha who comes out to greet Him. That is noteworthy, for she was the one we often think of as ‘the drudge’ - the one who was kitchen-bound - while her sister Mary would leave everything to sit at Jesus’ feet, washing them with precious perfume and wiping them with her hair while absorbing everything He said. Today, Mary would be prominent in Christian activity - president of the local Women’s Adoration Group while her sister would be in the background making coffee and serving cookies.

Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you had been here my brother would not have died” (John 11:21). Jesus assures her that her brother will live again, for He is the resurrection and the life.

I do not hear any condemnation in Martha's comment, just sadness. She then goes to Mary, to ask her to come to Jesus.

But why isn’t Mary already there? Surely, she knows that He is coming? Everyone would be aware of that, but Mary sat still in the house. Why? May I suggest that she was pouting!

She was offended ! When she comes to Jesus, she falls before Him weeping and says the same words as Martha had. “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died” (John 11:32).

Note that Jesus does not say the same comforting words to Mary that He expressed to her sister. Could this have been because of the tone of her voice? Accusing? Judgemental?

Instead of comforting Mary, “Jesus wept” (John 11:35), but not because Lazarus was dead - He had known that for some time and also that, in a short while, all would be rejoicing at his resurrection. He didn’t weep because Mary, Martha, and their friends were in sorrow - He had known that they would be for that was natural at the death of a loved one.

He wept because Mary was offended.

Jesus would die for our “offenses,” but He still grieves when we take offense.

On the journey to Bethany, Jesus had told His disciples that people are often offended when they cannot understand. They are walking in the dark (John 11:10). Had He known how Mary would react?

Why Offenses Come

Why does the Lord allow offenses to come? Could it be that His purpose is to reveal to us something about ourselves? Did John have to realize that, though he had declared that, “He must increase, and I must decrease” (John 3:30), that the timetable has to be the Lord’s not his.

It’s easy for us to fall into the trap of trying to manipulate God into doing things our way. It’s too easy to cross the line between accomplishing His will, versus our will. We must not get offended when He doesn’t do things ‘our way’ because only He knows what is best for us, even when we cannot see the reasons for the valleys we experience.

Did Mary need to learn that obedience and trust is far better than prominence and popularity, even in the Lord’s ‘service?’

Greatness in the Kingdom comes to those who would be least, even as servants (Luke 9:48).

What to Do With Offenses

First, you must own it ! The offense is yours! Another has not sinned against you - you ‘took the monkey’ on your own shoulders, so throw it off - or carry it!

Next, examine it ! The Lord allowed it to come that it may teach you something about yourself.

I have had to learn some hard things this way, and I have given you some of the reasons for offenses in the previous chapter. You must study your personality types and learn to major on your strengths. For example, most pastors tend to be melancholics. One gift of the melancholic is the ability to see problems long before others do. This can cause them to be critical of others, offended by their inability to see ‘the obvious,’ and to do something about it. Thank God you are not all like me!

Everybody’s giftings are different. For many years I was offended by others’ failure to recognize my teaching as a ‘gift.’ Everyone thinks they can teach, and I have had to learn to be ‘thick skinned’ when people ignore my giftings and calling as a pastor.

Once you have owned it and examined it , discard it !

By choice, pray about it and bury it! Bless those who have offended you and seek the empowering of the Holy Spirit if the offense seems too heavy - He has promised to be sufficient for all your trials.

“Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord. See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no ‘root of bitterness’ springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled” (Hebrews 12:14-15).

Then, the last step to take when the monkeys are on your shoulders, is to forget it ! Do not let the offense dwell in your heart any longer. Hand it off to the Lord, and let it off of your mind and heart.

Finally, do not be the one who causes offense , for, “woe to him through whom they come!” (Luke 17:1)!
